notes.1a: (i) The table was challenging as there were several variables to consider but most candidates were awarded full marks for drawing the table. In some cases, candidates did not provide suitable headings or units. It is important that candidates do not include units in the body of the table. Some candidates chose to draw three separate tables which is not appropriate.
notes.1aii: Most candidates drew suitable graphs from their tables with three separate lines for 1, 3 and 7 tubes. Axes were generally correctly labelled and matched the headings in their tables. There were a large number of points to plot, and many did this with accuracy. Candidates should use a scale that allows the plots to use at least 50% of the available space. When drawing a line of best fit, candidates should not go through the first and last point as a matter of course, but only when its suitable for the data. A small number of candidates extrapolated lines past their last point, which is not appropriate.
notes.1iii: Candidates were required to draw a conclusion based on their results. Many simply restated the trends or data from their practical. It is important that candidates practice the skill of thinking more holistically about the data and make overarching conclusions. Stronger responses recognised that huddling reduces heat loss. A number of candidates simply gave the reverse of their first conclusion for their second conclusion.
notes.1iv: In this question, candidates were asked to name two variables that were kept constant in the investigation. The most common answers were the volume of water and the temperature, both of which were not controlled.
notes.1v: Providing two suitable errors for the investigation proved challenging for many candidates. Many were able to demonstrate a vague understanding of a suitable error but did not give enough detail to be awarded the mark. Simply stating the tubes were only half filled is not the same as saying the volume of water was not accurately measured. �PAGE�42
notes.1vvi: When asked to give an improvement, many were able to recognise the need to measure the volume of water or the starting temperature, but many failed to qualify this by keeping it the same. A small number of candidates simply stated to use a thermostatically controlled water-bath. Candidates are encouraged to think carefully about the experiment and describe a relevant improvement rather than a generic improvement.
notes.1vii: Almost all candidates were able to name hot water or glass as a hazard.
notes.1b: The majority of responses described changing the temperature of amylase, while controlling the volume and concentration of starch and amylase solutions. A small number of candidates discussed using small mammals in experimentation which is not appropriate. Candidates are reminded to read the question carefully so that they interpret more accurately what is being asked of them. Most candidates also included the need for repeats, although a few did not state that two further repeats were necessary. Safety precautions were well known.
notes.2a: (i) Most answers referred to accuracy, rather than making it more representative or more reliable. An understanding of the key practical terms is important.
notes.2aii: Most candidates gained two marks on this question. A few were able to give a correct value between 3.2 and 3.4, but some did not indicate on the graph how they determined their value.
notes.2iii: Many candidates were able to gain at least two marks on this calculation. It is important that candidates practice percentage increase calculations and learn how to express their answers to the correct number of significant figures. It was clear that a few candidates were confused by significant figures and decimal places.
notes.2b: A wide range of correct answers were accepted, and most candidates were able to give a value in the correct range. Fewer gave the correct unit.
notes.2c: Many candidates correctly identified the need to use Benedict’s reagent for the reducing sugar test and that the colour change would be from blue to brick red.
notes.2d: This question assessed candidates’ ability to produce a standard biological drawing, following all necessary conventions. Candidates must be able to produce a drawing using a sharp pencil that has clear and continuous lines. It is important that candidates do not use shading and that they correctly follow the instructions in the question. Many candidates were not able to gain full marks as their leaf veins extended outside the margin of the leaf. Another common error was not including a vein in each lobe.
notes.2e: Candidates were asked to provide one similarity and one difference between the leaves. The most common similarity was that the leaf had five sections. Gaining the mark for the difference was more challenging. Some simply stated a characteristic of one leaf rather than making a suitable comparative statement. �PAGE�43
notes.key_messages:
Candidates should manage their time so that they are able to complete the practical activity but also have
enough time to complete all questions.
Candidates should ensure that they read the questions carefully before starting to answer. This is particularly
important for any planning exercise that is required. Identification of the dependent and independent variables
is vital before a plan is completed. Controlled variables must also be considered and included in a plan.
Candidates should also try to match the answers they give with the number of marks available for each part
of a question. A three-mark question will require three separate points to be made if full credit is to be awarded.
notes.general_comments:
Most candidates performed well on this paper, with good answers seen in many cases. It is essential that all
questions are attempted, even if the candidate is unsure of the answer as they may gain partial credit even if
full marks are not awarded.
